The metric dimension of a graph has been a well-studied concept with a wide range of applications, capturing a graph's uniqueness properties. Given a set of walkers starting on vertices of a graph, their paths can be distinguished based on the distances they traverse, enabling the identification of the starting locations. However, in many scenarios, reducing the amount of data collected by the walkers can still accurately determine their original positions. To address this challenge, a new parameter called the shortened metric dimension (SMD) is introduced, incorporating the minimum number required nodes be observed at in order to determine the original starting location of N distinct walkers after a specified number of steps. The paper that introduced this concept explores its various aspects, determining its relationship to existing parameters, identifying its structure, and providing specific values for popular graphs. Theoretical contributions also include optimization problems and the graph structure required for minimum values of SMD. The research demonstrates a practical application of SMD in decoding error correction algorithms. In a scenario with three or more agents, where each agent takes individual turns making offers in a negotiation, we are examining the possibility of improving the resulting allocation of values through the introduction of a rule that governs their behavior. Specifically, we are exploring whether there exists a suitable mechanism that, when followed by the agents, could lead to a more efficient allocation of values than is achieved in a standard sequential bargaining setting. Our investigation shows that, indeed, such a mechanism does exist, and it can be designed to yield outcomes that are, in fact, more desirable than those obtained in a serial bargaining model. Furthermore, this mechanism can be applied to a broad range of situations, not limited to large groups of agents. Additionally, we are demonstrating that this mechanism's ability to generate more efficient outcomes holds true when considering other relevant criteria, such as its ability to fairly treat all the involved parties. So much so, that there exists a particular group of situations, called the class of environments with single-peaked preferences, where this mechanism not only yields more desirable outcomes but also does so in a way that treats all parties fairly. So, to summarize, we have discovered a suitable mechanism that, when followed by the involved parties, leads to a more efficient allocation of values, fair to all, and this mechanism's benefits hold true for a broad range of situations, including large groups of agents. The presence of topological constraints in proteins' three-dimensional structures makes their bending highly unpredictable unless additional information is used. Recent advances in visualizing the inner structure of knotted proteins through MRI technology have generated 3D models with precise spatial information, allowing for a direct observation of their internal topological features. By applying persistent homology to these models, we are able to identify the spatial arrangement of their twisted components and provide a computational framework that can forecast the bending patterns of these proteins based on their internal topology, rejecting the need for assumptions about their flexible behavior. Our model's predictions were tested on a set of knotted proteins and revealed a distinct pattern of bending preferences along their molecular chains, reflected in the spatial distribution of their twisted components. The analysis of these patterns reveals a combination of local and global topological effects that influence the bending of knotted proteins and their ability to bind with specific partners. Our study demonstrates the practical application of persistent homology in analyzing the spatial relationships in proteins and provides a significant biological insight into the relationship between the internal topology of knotted proteins and their flexible behavior. Recent advancements in large language models have enabled the creation of counterfactual language models that can generate alternative descriptions of given sentences. However, producing high-quality counterfactuals consistently has been a major challenge, especially when it comes to phrasal-level modifications. Current approaches tend to focus primarily on categorical changes, neglecting the complex web of local relationships within a sentence. In response to this limitation, we propose a novel task and matching evaluation methodology for counterfactual language models to assess the ability to preserve both a sentence's original meaning and its internal structural connections. We establish a baseline using contrastive training on top of BART and T5, and also design a series of rigorous evaluation experiments to evaluate the models' performance. Our results indicate a strong correlation between evaluating counterfactual models using meaning preservation and structural preservation as separate criteria. Ultimately, we demonstrate that finely-tuned pre-trained language models can effectively generate high-quality counterfactuals, surpassing the performance of low-resource models and achieving a score of 21.8% on the FCPF evaluation metric. Our research concludes with an examination of the challenges ahead, including the development of more sophisticated assessment tools to guide future model improvements. Our model's code is available at https://github.com/nyuogroup/Disco.

In real-world applications, instances are frequently categorized into multiple labels by being described with multiple features. For example in image classification, a picture that includes both an animal and a vehicle would likely have distinct visual characteristics than an image featuring just an animal. While multi-label learning problems are often addressed with various algorithms, many remain agnostic to this inherent relationship between labels. In contrast, we propose a method called Multi-Label Relationship Learning (MLRL), which leverages information about the intrinsic connections between labels by making effective use of individual positive instances. MLRL incorporates a novel module called Relation Awareness Network (RAN) to enable explicit consideration of label relationships. We further investigate how natural language descriptions of individual positive instances can be utilized to uncover these relationships, resulting in MLRL-D (Data) and MLRL-DN (Noise), both of which incorporate RAN. Experimental evaluations on realistic multi-label datasets showing natural feature descriptions demonstrate MLRL's benefits in accurately modeling label relationships and MLRL-DN's ability to handle noisy instance descriptions. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose. The proliferation of wearable devices and mobile apps for health monitoring has generated a vast amount of data, making it desirable to conduct statistical analysis without requiring these devices to transfer private data to a central location. Utilizing machine learning models on this local data remains a challenge. Typically, research focuses on developing algorithms within a centralized framework, ignoring the possibilities of federated or transfer learning. In response, we design a novel architecture called FedHealth, integrating principles of federated learning and transfer learning. It enables the construction of personalized models on client devices while considering data diversity. Weoretical proofs of FedHealth's performance advantages are provided, along with a detailed experimental evaluation of our method. Our findings, obtained using real data from the Google Fit app, demonstrate FedHealth's efficacy compared to alternative approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/PrashantA1/FedHealth.

This study tackles a control problem where the cost function is composed of two parts, one of which involves a switching cost, and the other, which can be determined through observation, may include delays. The goal is to minimize costs while maximizing the time spent in certain states. The problem is complex due to the presence of state constraints, sharp corners in the state space, and the possibility of observing the state with time lags. The key challenge lies in handling the switching cost, which hinders the use of the familiar "reverse" method. The problem is initially formulated in the framework of a stopping time, but this leads to issues with verifying the uniqueness of the solution, especially in the presence of unbounded costs and sudden changes in the state. The problem is then recast as a stochastic control problem with a state constraint, but the presence of switching costs creates difficulties with differentiating the value function, which results in the problem being equivalent to the initial problem with the cost function being the solution to the HJB equation. The problem is further analyzed by applying the "reverse" method to the cost function, which provides an integral form of the solution. The problem of finding the solution to the HJB equation is then reformulated as a quasi-variational differential game, which can be solved by applying dynamic programming. The solution is then expressed in terms of the first exit time from a half-space, which is the key to understanding the solution. The paper also explores three special cases, one with bounded costs, one with small costs, and one with a specific state constraint. The solutions to these special cases provide valuable insights into the solution to the general problem. The paper also presents numerical methods for computing the solution to the general problem. To explore the potential of lepton-quark duality, we examine the production of a specific pair of leptoquark types - denoted as (1,0) and (0,1) - which have opposite charge properties. By analyzing their pair production, we can identify distinct patterns that could aid in identifying these particles. A comprehensive investigation of these patterns is conducted, considering various combinations of lepton and quark pairs. For instance, producing a pair of electrons and u-quarks exhibits the same charge asymmetry as producing a pair of muons and d-quarks. Furthermore, by matching theoretical predictions to available LHC data, we can estimate the mass range of these leptoquark pairs. In this work, we address a critical issue in causal neural learning, specifically within the framework proposed by Pearl (2018), where the relationship between inputs and outputs is defined through observables and latent variables. The problem arises when the model is unable to discern between certain input configurations that have different effects on the outcome due to the presence of confounding factors. Our contribution is two-fold: we develop a method (Causal Neural Network Re-identification, CNNR) that detects and disentangles hidden variables from neural networks, and we demonstrate how this capability enables the efficient identification of causal relationships by validating our approach on synthetic and real-world data. The problem of erroneous positives in visual association detection is a growing concern, causing issues for applications in security, driving, and other fields. Humans have an easy time identifying the association between images, but current computer-based methods struggle to match this level of performance. A significant portion of incorrect responses can be attributed to the presence of distracting background elements in one or both images. In this research, we focus on developing a method to minimize the effect of background distractions and enhance the accuracy of visual association detection. To effectively deal with scenarios involving complex backgrounds and various image sizes and orientations, we introduce a new transformation called spatial-aware horizontal flipping. This flipping strategy can be incorporated into existing neural network-based methods without significant modifications, as it does not alter the network architecture. To illustrate the benefits of this technique, we implemented it in a conventional ResNet-based model and demonstrated its advantages in both the VGG16 and Inception-based models. The resulting method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the VGG16 and Inception-based models in the VCD dataset and matches the performance of these models on the CVC-12 dataset. Moreover, this method delivers superior performance in real-world driving scenarios, as observed in a driving environment test. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrasoul/Spatial-Aware-Floating.

The observation of a rapidly spinning (104 days) 13.2 mag K2 giant star, HS Os, presents a puzzle because angular momentum conservation suggests its planetry nature is unlikely. To explain this contradiction, researchers have several possible scenarios, including the presence of massive absorbing planets, or an unknown internal or external angular momentum source within the star itself. To test these hypotheses, we calculated the expected period changes for a range of possible planets with different masses, orbital periods, and eccentricities. If the star continues at its present rate of spin-down, a team found that any substantial planet would need a significant eccentricity to avoid being detected, although most current models struggle to account for the observed spin. Alternatively, a scenario known as spin-up by mass inflow, where the star is gaining mass and angular momentum from an unknown source, could also fit the data. To differentiate between these hypotheses, future observations are necessary to determine the stellar radius, which in turn will help in determining the planetary parameters. Additionally, detecting a planetary tidal signature in the star's light curves or determining the presence of a massive inflow rate could provide more information about the underlying dynamics. Despite the uncertainties, HS Os offers a unique case study that can contribute to a better comprehension of the angular momentum conservation within stars and their planets. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate how the Baez-Duarte-Hopkins-Weiss-Miller construction leads to the identification of specific subgroups within the homotopy groups of infinite complex projective spaces. By applying this approach, we derive insights into the composition of these groups and reveal their structured elements, thereby establishing a connection to the concept of rooted trees. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the space defined by infinite graded projective complexes and the space formed by rooted trees, demonstrating that this relationship can be expressed in terms of a structured group called the group of rooted trees, to a high level of precision. Additionally, we explore the implications of this discovery for the fundamental group of infinite complex projective spaces, revealing that it is composed of a specific type of element called branchings, and we provide a graphical representation of this structure. Lastly, we outline a potential line of inquiry related to the study of the group of rooted trees.

A significant challenge in hyper-spectral image classification exists due to cerebral lesions that greatly distort the spectral information. To address this, a new technique called Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-encoder (PAVAE) has been developed to automatically identify and remove lesions from HSIs. The PAVAE network consists of multiple VAE components working together, starting with a preliminary estimation of lesion masks based on intensity information, followed by two additional refinement stages that employ adversarial and cat-and-dog encoders to produce more accurate results. The resulting encoder learns a compact and efficient representation of images with removed lesions, leading to a significant improvement in classification performance. Evaluations using real-world images demonstrate the effectiveness of PAVAE, showing a notable increase of up to 12% in accuracy compared to current lesion removal methods. Moreover, the encoded features obtained from the encoder are valuable for other applications, such as noise reduction and data compression, demonstrating the broad potential of PAVAE. Working with categorical data for modeling and prediction tasks is common practice. Categorical variables can be represented as binary matrices, comprising a separate column for each category. When dealing with sparse models, incorporating categorical data can lead to overfitting, especially in high-dimensional scenarios. The Group Lasso, also known as the L1-regularized group sparse model, has been effective in reducing overfitting while extracting meaningful information from continuous and categorical data. However, the computational time increases substantially when applying the Group Lasso directly to high-dimensional categorical data, rendering it impractical for real-world applications. To overcome this challenge, we propose an efficient alternative, the Adaptive Group Lasso, consisting of two stages. In the pre-processing stage, we apply the adaptive Group Lasso to obtain a compact set of relevant features. These selected features are then used to determine the optimal lambda value for the standard Group Lasso in the post-processing stage. We also derive a theoretical guarantee for the Adaptive Group Lasso, demonstrating that it yields an estimation error bounded by a constant times the minimal number of dimensions, as the strongest relevant column becomes sufficiently small. Moreover, the Adaptive Group Lasso achieves a consistent estimation performance, backed by both theoretical and numerical evidence. The proposed method excels in handling high-dimensional categorical data and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various simulation studies. The efficacy of the Adaptive Group Lasso is further demonstrated through a real-data example, showcasing its practical applications. The code associated with the Adaptive Group Lasso is publicly available on GitHub. The results presented in this paper extend previously known theoretical guarantees under a weaker sparsity condition, specifically requiring that the strongest relevant column be bounded by a constant times the square root of the number of dimensions. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks, yet they struggle with complex, real-world scenarios, such as text-based reinforcement learning and conversational games, that demand a high level of structure and organization. To overcome this limitation, our approach develops a method called Structured Insight Infusion for Large Language Models, that infuses structured knowledge into LLMs through targeted attention mechanisms, enabling them to effectively utilize their inherent contextual understanding. We apply this method to a variety of challenging tasks, including text-based reinforcement learning, conversational games, and multi-step reasoning, and find that it consistently boosts the performance of pre-trained LLMs. When compared to other strengthening methods, our approach demonstrates significant gains, averaging a 13% improvement in problem-solving efficiency. Additionally, our method showcases a high degree of adaptability, allowing it to be effectively integrated into existing training protocols. We open-source the code for our method, along with comprehensive experimentation results, to facilitate further research and development.

To address this issue, this research introduces an innovative technique for achieving aesthetically pleasing anti-aliasing in line connections on vector maps, while maintaining efficiency for real-time rendering. Unlike existing methods that prioritize performance over visual quality, our approach leverages a sophisticated analysis of display aliasing, grid sampling patterns, and Fourier analysis to provide a more visually acceptable result. To accommodate performance demands, the algorithm is designed to operate within a limited set of common display resolutions. To accommodate different rendering requirements, our technique can be applied to either 2D line connections or more complex scenes featuring 3D polygons. Our solution has been implemented on top of CesiumJS, a renowned 3D globe rendering engine, and evaluation results reveal its capability to yield high-quality anti-aliasing effects while maintaining low computational overhead. Experimental data obtained from various devices and scenes demonstrate our approach's effectiveness, also highlighting its broad compatibility with popular rendering engines. To facilitate easy adoption, the anti-aliasing source code has been made available on GitHub under the permissive Apache-2 license. Further, a derivate of the algorithm called "Line AA" has been created, which provides a simplified yet efficient anti-aliasing solution for line connections, capable of being incorporated into various rendering frameworks. Experimental evaluations conducted on mobile devices revealed Line AA's low overhead, amounting to approximately 10-20 milliseconds. To expand the approach's applicability, researchers have explored its compatibility with vector map editing tools, discovering ways to integrate the algorithm with CesiumJS and Three.js to yield anti-aliasing effects in real-time, also finding it possible to achieve similar results with lower overhead using WebGL directly. In multi-channel speech processing, improving the quality of individual channels can significantly benefit source separation and speech enhancement tasks. Recent studies have focused on model-based and map-domain individual channel speech improvement approaches. This paper introduces the DPCRN model, a dual-path network that combines convolutional and recurrent elements to effectively restore individual channels. The proposed DPCRN architecture consists of a feature transformation block, a dual-path network, and a combination block. Experiments conducted on multi-channel speech enhancement tasks using the Interspeech 2020 deep-sumering network dataset and the 6-channel speech enhancement dataset showed that the DPCRN model achieves superior results compared to baseline methods. Code for the DPCRN model is available online at: https://github.com/ling Xu/DPCRN. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this paper, we gather a dataset that includes 15,000 freely available Twitter sentiment
classification posts. We then assemble a new set of 5000 training examples and 5000 testing
examples from this original dataset. Our novel approach to sentiment classification, based
on long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, consistently outperforms the established techniques
in our assessment. Our findings are backed by our results, which show an overall accuracy rate
of 87% in classifying the sentiment of unknown Twitter posts. Notably, our model excels at
detecting irritable language, accurately identifying 89% of negative tweets correctly. In the
process of conducting the experiment, we encountered an issue with an earlier version of
Keras, which we resolved by modifying the LSTM model to include a dropout layer. Our code
is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/AmmarHelmi/Twitter-Sentiment-Analysis.

We introduce the concept of a hyperlayer, a higher-level approximation that excels at limiting a model's capabilities. A model's capacity to pass a specific dataset screening test is studied by incorporating hyperlayers, and we find that the presence of a dataset with varying scale sizes hinders the effectiveness to some degree. Furthermore, we discovered a relationship between the size of the dataset and the level of decoupling required to achieve a certain level of effectiveness. Additionally, we found that the presence of noise in the input data complicates the assessment of the model's ability to exclude certain samples. The model's ability to accomplish a task on a different dataset is predicted by analyzing its ability to succeed on a smaller, similar dataset. The principle of restricting a model's effectiveness can be applied to various contexts, including but not limited to, protecting sensitive information, eliminating misleading data, and detecting anomalies. The approach presented in this paper provides a quantitative metric that can be utilized in the development, validation, and assessment of deep learning models, particularly in situations involving screening and the exclusion of irrelevant data. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through effective knowledge transfer. We have identified two main approaches for transferring knowledge: (1) incorporating expert guidance, and (2) modifying the environment to reflect successful experiences. While these methods are beneficial, they require the expertise or modified environment to be accessible, which is not always the case. This research introduces a robust knowledge transfer framework that enables the agent to transfer knowledge without any additional information about the target environment. It achieves this by training the agent on a diverse set of diverse tasks, which acts as a representative model for general knowledge. When applied to a new, unseen task, the agent is able to utilize this representative model effectively, resulting in enhanced performance. Our approach has been successfully tested on various tasks, including complex games like Procurement and Cartpole, and has been compared to other knowledge transfer methods with notable results. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ghru/zero-shot-knowledge-transfer.

An investigation of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ decays is conducted, with specific focus on identifying $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ modes and calculating their branching fractions with subsequent $D\to KK$ decays. We analyze the connection between action space size and the neural network's output, showing that the large action space leads to overfitting, continuous output values, and difficulty in convergence. To address this issue, we propose a novel exploration method, a new training objective, and a strategy to increase the embedding dimension. We also explore the impact of various techniques, such as label smoothing, dropout, and clipping, on the action space. Our experiments on WMT English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks show that our proposed methods consistently outperform the baseline, achieving new state-of-the-art performance. We publicly share our code to facilitate further research. The discussion is accompanied by visualizations of our findings, and we outline potential future work along with them. The paper is structured as follows: we begin with an overview of neural machine translation, followed by analyses of action spaces, exploration, and regularization, before describing our proposed methods, experiments, and case studies, and finally, we conclude the discussion.

Thanks to speech-emotion-based applications such as human-computer interaction and fraud detection, identifying speech emotions has become a highly sought-after capability in recent times. Our approach is particularly effective in adapting to new domains with limited data, as seen in the results of our additional experiments conducted on the EMODB dataset. In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have seen significant improvements in generating coherent and realistic texts. These achievements are particularly evident in natural language processing tasks such as text classification, where GANs are used to augment training data by creating novel texts. However, existing approaches often fail to account for an intelligent, strategic adversary that would manipulate the data generation process for malicious purposes. To address this shortcoming, we introduce SparseGAN, a new framework that enables a less restrictive adversary by considering a competing, intelligent opponent that is capable of adjusting its behavior to thwart the model's performance. In various experiments, SparseGAN demonstrated its versatility in generating high-quality texts and its ability to outperform baseline models in tasks like sentiment analysis. Furthermore, we discovered that training a sparse adversary leads to a more challenging text generation task, requiring the model to produce more diverse and complex texts. SparseGAN's source code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

Manganese nitride thin films, represented by the example Mn$_3$NiN, exhibit unusual magnetic properties depending on the amount of oxygen present, switching from a stable pattern of Néel and Bloch walls in an antiferromagnetic arrangement with oxygen, to a more complex and dynamic pattern of magnetic domains without oxygen. Animal observations play a significant role in forming the foundation of various ecological theories and have continuous applications in fields like forestry, wildlife conservation, and management.  However, gathering data on certain species, particularly those in remote areas with little access to video footage, proves to be extremely challenging and time-consuming.  A significant amount of movement of these animals falls within the'slow movement' category, which poses a problem for existing automatic detection methods, given their predisposition for responding to rapid movement.  This report introduces an innovative, fully automatic method for detecting the movement of animals at a slow pace, specifically in video footage captured in the wild, with an emphasis on birds and large forest mammals.  The newly developed technique, along with a specially designed dataset, has been put to use in detecting the movement of certain bird species, prior to being extended to a broader range of birds, in addition to large forest mammals.  The developed system has a user-friendly interface that allows for easy data collection, while the method itself has been made available on an open source platform. The obtained results demonstrate that this method has a high level of accuracy, as shown by both the accuracy of the created map of elephant movement and the precise matching of their natural habits.  This report concludes by highlighting the potential applications and future development of this method, which could be further enhanced by integrating it with machine learning algorithms.  This could be achieved by either training the existing system on a larger dataset, or by creating a new system from scratch, along with a discussion on different possible learning algorithms and various dataset considerations.  The report also presents a proposed plan for conducting similar trials in other parts of India, which have different geographical characteristics, in addition to providing some graphs and figures related to the movement of elephants. The abstract representation of environment interactions provides valuable insights for designers of legged robots, and the research also contributes to a better understanding of the key elements involved in safe and stable landing. In dense stellar matter, we examine the structure of strange quark matter with self-bound compact stars and meson-dressed dense stars at high density.  Our analysis focuses on the sound speed, which is crucial in pinpointing the characteristics of these stars.  Our main findings regarding the sound speed in these contexts are as follows:  (1)  The sound speed in strange quark matter is fixed at approximately 0.46, independent of density.  (2)  We can divide dense stars made of strange quark matter into three categories based on their density:  (a)  Those with densityless strange quark matter where the sound speed can be calculated using a one-loop QCD approximation, (b)  Self-bound strange quark stars at intermediate densities, and (c)  High-density stars where the sound speed approaches 0.46.  (3)  We also determine the density at which the sound speed stops increasing and begins to approach 0.46, finding it to be approximately 4.4 times (1.85) dense than nuclear matter density for self-bound (massive) strange quark stars.  (4)  The sound speed in meson-dressed dense stars lies between 0.46 and 0.5, depending on the meson's mass.  (5)  Our analysis indicates that the sound speed is more effective than baryon number density in distinguishing compact stars made of strange quark matter, as it directly relates to the underlying physics of these objects.  Consequently, we propose a new criterion for identifying strange quark stars, specifically that their sound speed must be greater than 0.46 everywhere.  This discovery also implies that strange quark stars cannot be modeled as uniform objects, as this would result in a sound speed of 0.46 everywhere, and instead they must be composed of different density regions.  Our research provides a sound speed vs. density pattern that can be used to better understand the properties of strange quark matter and the structure of strange quark stars.  This pattern can be distinguished in data obtained from future observations of compact stars made of strange quark matter, specifically through the study of oscillations around equilibrium, which would allow us to probe the sound speed throughout these stars. Despite its success, knowledge tracing faces challenges, and researchers continually seek to improve it. Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on large amounts of data for fine-tuning. However, correcting grammatical errors in new domains often involves accessing limited data. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a domain adaptation technique that leverages a small amount of labeled data from a new domain for explicit mapping, enabling efficient domain transfer. The proposed framework, consisting of a controller and a set of domain-specific controllers, enables the model to learn a general representation that can be finely tuned for new domains. Experimental evaluations on NME and BLEU metrics demonstrate significant improvements over baseline models in five target domains. Furthermore, the model exhibits high adaptability when transferred to new, unlabeled domains, including student essays from the TOEFL test. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenXudong14/GEDT.

The problem of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested and rational agents, who engage in pairwise interactions and make independent decisions, presents an significant challenge. In this context, finding an allocation that is both fair and maximizes total utility, is difficult to achieve. A recent study demonstrated that, under certain conditions, it's possible to design a mechanism that produces a fair and efficient Pure Nash Equilibrium. However, this equilibrium may not be equitable in the sense of Roughly Fair Allocation (RFA), which considers the relative satisfaction of each agent. In the present work, we investigate RFA-equipped mechanisms that guarantee the existence of an equitable Pure Nash Equilibrium for single-parameter environments. Additionally, we show that these mechanisms yield an equilibrium that is not only fair but also ensures that the distance between the utilities of any two agents remains relatively small. This implies a level of diffusion among the agents' utilities, which has no precedent in the existing literature. Furthermore, we provide lower and upper bounds on the fairness-induced loss when considering two-types of agents, showing that there is no gap between these bounds. Lastly, we provide relevant theoretical and experimental analysis of two-specific models. The salient features of these models, which lead to equitable and efficient Nash Equilibria, can be identified. The code for the experiments is publicly available. Evaluating the range of accretion rates in young stars is crucial for validating the disk-regulation mechanism thought to contribute to the formation of low-mass stars. While most T Tauri stars exhibit similar accretion and rotation patterns, some, like XX Cha, demonstrate exceptional accretion fluctuations. Our analysis of XX Cha, based on a revised dataset including new spectroscopic measurements, reveals unusually large accretion rate variations, spanning over an order of magnitude, and distinct rotational modulation components. We interpret these findings within the context of recent star-formation models and a grid of shell-based spectrum simulations, also considering the effects of viewing geometry and mass-loss. Compared to other T Tauri stars with similar masses and ages, XX Cha shows significantly higher-than-expected accretion rates, which we attribute to its documented high-specific-angular-momentum. This, in turn, may be the result of a misaligned rotation axis and an unusually large disk. Furthermore, our analysis of XX Cha's dataset reveals evidence of accretion fluctuations on much shorter timescales, which, along with similar findings in other stars, may be explained by turbulence in the disk. Lastly, our research emphasizes the significance of continuous observational records in defining the range of accretion rates in young stars. Given the limited nature of the current database, which primarily consists of sporadic measurements, we cannot confidently assert that the documented range of accretion rates in T Tauri stars extends far beyond a factor of ten. Essentially, any proposed disk-regulation mechanism must be capable of accommodating this possible extent in order to be considered valid. Given current understanding, any such mechanism would require a complex interplay with migration and turbulence within the disk. Lastly, accurate determinations of accretion rates depend heavily on accurate determinations of hydrogen lines, which, in their turn, rely on accurate reddening corrections. The notion of single-particle entanglement is often misinterpreted, as it can be seen as a form of two-particle correlation. To examine this, we studied an infinite, one-dimensional Bose system with periodic boundary conditions using a semi-Heisenberg chain to identify the conditions under which single-particle entanglement leads to the guidance of another particle at the other end of the chain. Our analysis shows that in a non-interacting Bose system, the lack of pair correlations allows for single-particle entanglement, which results in the genuine nonlocal effect of particle guidance. Furthermore, as the level of interaction increases, the decay of pair correlations always leads to single-particle entanglement causing nonlocal effects, which can also lead to the exchange of particle guidance in both directions. Additionally, we found that in a closed system, single-particle entanglement ultimately breaks down at a certain critical distance as the system reaches thermal equilibrium. Moreover, in an open system with a reservoir at thermal equilibrium, we found that single-particle entanglement persists for all distances, yet it decreases with distance due to its relationship with pair correlations. Lastly, our analysis demonstrated how the lack of pair correlations allows for single-particle entanglement, which results in the nonlocal effect of particle guidance, offering a tangible, measurable consequence of single-particle entanglement. In FDD systems, codebooks for precoder and feedback encoding are often created independently, without regard for the baseband signal characteristics. This research explores the benefits of codebook construction and feedback encoding being mutually informative, resulting in improved encoding and decoding efficiency. A proposed method develops codebooks and feedback bits in tandem, leveraging Gaussian Mixture Models to accurately model baseband signals. This approach leads to codebooks and feedback bits that are not only more accurate, but also significantly more compact, resulting in, e.g. a codebook reduction of 85.6% in a real-world scenario, along with corresponding decreases in encoding and decoding overhead. Consequently, this approach provides a valuable technique for reducing codeword and feedback storage, as well as associated processing, transmission, and reception expenses, especially in scenarios with limited memory. In such cases, the proposed method can be beneficial, yielding further gains when implemented on top of existing compression techniques. Experimental results validate the proposed method's effectiveness across various signal conditions and applications. In particular, codebook reduction factors ranging from 53.4 to 97.3% were observed, depending on the environment, without a corresponding decrease in encoding and decoding accuracy. In fact, in some instances, a slight improvement, e.g. 2.8% in one example, was observed. In addition to codebook reduction, the proposed method provides valuable information that can be used for other purposes, such as channel estimation, interference mitigation, and cell loading, also yielding further gains, as shown in one example where the proposed method led to a 10.8% increase in codewords supported in a real-world scenario. In general, the method can be applied to any FDD system, including but not limited to 5G base stations, access points, and satellite communication systems, among others. Moreover, the proposed method offers design guidelines for various environments, facilitating easy adaptation, as demonstrated in four distinct scenarios. Furthermore, the method's impact on user experience was investigated, resulting in no observable impact on delay, throughput, or overall experience, according to various metrics including, but not limited to, E2E delay, data transmission rate, and overall system performance, in real-world scenarios, including, but not limited to, five different 5G scenarios. In conclusion, the proposed method provides a valuable technique with wide-ranging applications, offering further gains in other metrics, as shown in the results. Researchers proposed the Bondi mass asymptotically describes a system's mass near infinity. However, defining a physically meaningful approach to calculate this asymptotic mass is challenging due to the requirements for an expanding coordinate system and complete reliability of the infinite data. Presently, an alternative is using conformal coordinate systems, which yield the arctan Bondi mass, exhibiting a more manageable and physically significant parameter in analyses of asymptotic masses. A key advantage of this approach is the unambiguous identification of asymptotic masses for systems lacking infinite reliability, such as certain black hole mergers. By utilizing advanced numerical simulations of mergers, the authors established a relationship between the arctan Bondi mass and the total energy released during the merger, which can be utilized in identifying physically credible Bondi mass reductions, specifically less than 2.4% for mergers similar to GW150914. Additionally, a related analysis of the curvature scalar near infinity, which is independent of coordinate systems, also indicates that the rate of change in this quantity is restricted to a certain extent, specifically less than 4.5% for mergers similar to GW150914. These findings have implications for theories such as quantum gravity and asymptotic simplicity, which dictate that systems lacking infinite reliability must have minimal change in their asymptotic properties. Furthermore, these results provide a non-trivial prediction for future detections of mergers similar to GW150914, with detectability via the curvature scalar near infinity, which can be extracted from LIGO data via a new method developed by the authors. Similarly, another new method developed by the authors for analyzing LIGO data via the arctan Bondi mass discovered another non-trivial prediction concerning the distribution of the energy released during the mergers of superdense objects similar to GW150914, which should be investigated in a forthcoming paper. In this study, we aim to enhance the physical layer security of an OFDM-based wireless system that employs a single RF party relay. The findings obtained can be applied to various scenarios, including 5G and next-generation wireless systems, by implementing a secure and efficient relay node. The study also highlights the potential applications of OFDM-based D2D communication, cellular networks, and relay-based wireless systems, across different frequencies, such as sub-6 GHz, millimeter wave, and THz frequencies, in various scenarios, including urban, suburban, and rural environments. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 moves per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million moves per second, allowing for extensive tests involving large numbers of agents. 
To demonstrate the benefits of this enhanced platform, we conducted a series of experiments involving state-of-the-art text-based dialogue systems, showcasing the potential of TextWorldExpress for demanding evaluations. 
The express version of TextWorld is available at https://textworldexpress.com/.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static scenarios, uses a semi-relativistic approximation during the early stages of star formation, especially during periods of significant mass accumulation. Once the mass accumulation becomes negligible, the transition to a fully relativistic treatment is implemented. Our method involves using a set of quasi-static, semi-relativistic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations during this stage. By leveraging a convergence criterion, we can determine when to switch from the semi-relativistic to the fully relativistic equations. This approach yields the same results as the fully relativistic equations for low rotation rates, while producing rotation-induced oscillations similar to those obtained through direct solutions of the fully relativistic equations. Our algorithm has been applied to various rotation rates in stars with masses 1.2 and 1.4 solar masses, consisting of pure neutron star matter and pure pure meson-star matter. This led to the determination of mass limits for stability in these scenarios. Additionally, our method allows for the incorporation of other time-independent factors, such as magnetic fields, asymmetries, and composition gradients, that may influence the formation and evolution of rotating stars. Our proposed approach, referred to as Visual Document Extraction via Synthesis (VDES), introduces a new method for cost-effectively training high-performance models in extracting data from visually complex documents. We argue that utilizing supervised automatic labeling results in exorbitant labeling costs, primarily due to the extensive number of documents that require data mining. In response, VDES leverages a limited set of labeled documents to develop a style-specific model, enabling the generation of diverse unlabeled documents. These synthesized documents contain no errors but lack the unique characteristics of specific documents. By training the model on both real and synthesized data, we achieve significant reductions in labeling costs while still obtaining precise results. Our experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of VDES over the conventional approach. When working with invoices, we were able to decrease the labeling cost by approximately 97 percent. When processing insurance documents, we saw a more modest but still substantial reduction of 87 percent in labeling costs. Our code is available online at GitHub.

The Advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) and Virgo Collaborations observe the entire sky through a network of gravitational waves, allowing them to identify nearly all gravitational wave events. However, due to the limited field of view, not all events have corresponding electromagnetic counterparts observed in the sky. The number of counterparts that exist is substantial, making it a challenge to establish comprehensive catalogs. A neural network was trained to recognize gravitational waves produced by neutron star-binary mergers, distinguishing between low-mass and high-mass combinations, and determining the binary's orbital inclination. Applying this network to simulated signals resulted in accurate predictions, while a survey of nearly a decade's worth of LIGO data uncovered a few instances that matched the predicted signals, which were then compared to observed electromagnetic counterparts in the sky. Although most counterparts remain unknown, the network's capabilities could be refined to account for specific electromagnetic phenomena, thus potentially linking a significant number of currently unassociated counterparts to neutron star mergers. The code for this project is available online.

Recent public health measures aimed at mitigating COVID-19's transmission led to significant changes in how people interact with others in public. By analyzing a dataset from a mobility app, this study explores how urban interactions varied across different income groups in a major city. Our findings reveal that higher-income individuals reduced their mobility compared to lower-income individuals, contradicting general assumptions about how different socioeconomic groups respond to health crises. Furthermore, these individuals eventually resumed their pre-pandemic mobility patterns more quickly, taking less time to return to normal than expected, given the initial slowdown. In fact, their increased mobility in the later stages of the pandemic exceeded predictions, contributing to a longer-lasting decline in face-to-face interactions between people of different socioeconomic statuses. The formation of massive stars is a critical area for study as it is closely linked to the death of stars in supernovae and explosive events or dissipation of matter.  Yet, the precise mechanisms of massive star formation remain unclear due to lack of data on young massive stars.  One possible pathway to forming massive stars involves accumulating mass and angular momentum from molecular clouds, either by being stranded at the center of cloud collapse or through the absorption of high-density clumps.  Alternatively, these stars may form as a result of binary merger in a star-forming region.  Using submillimeter observations from HOPS, GBT-ARO, and ATLAS, we investigated the mass accumulation and star-forming history of two massive protostars located in the Taurus molecular cloud.  Our analysis of their mass spectra reveals that both protostars are in a stage of rapid mass accumulation through the consumption of clumps.  However, unlike the highly variable 40 km/s, the protostar L1521F-NTS is distinguished by having a nearly uniform mass spectrum with indications of being formed through cloud collapse.  In contrast, the spectrum of 40 km/s exhibits a power-law similar to that of low-mass protostars, suggesting it may have a different origin. The distinction between its mass spectra could also be linked to the presence of a disk, as modeled by numerical simulations. The collapse of both protostars is expected to result in massive star formation, with the possibility of one being a binary star and the other a rapidly rotating star. Our research employs density functional theory to examine the electronic and magnetic structure of rutile TiO2 when carbon or nitrogen is incorporated as a p-element. Our analysis covers various bond lengths, energy gaps, and magnetic moments for different arrangements of N or C within the TiO2 lattice. Our findings indicate that carbon typically forms a bond with an oxygen atom to form a CO dimer, resulting in a non-magnetic arrangement, whereas nitrogen can bond with a titanium atom in a tetrahedral configuration and exhibit both magnetic and semi-conductive properties, depending on its location. If the N is situated at a site where it can form a bond with an oxygen atom, it acts as a donor, leading to a semi-conductive arrangement, and when situated in a site where it can form a bond with a titanium atom in a tetrahedral configuration, it results in a magnetic and semi-conductive arrangement. Our study shows that nitrogen bonded to a titanium atom in a tetrahedral configuration exhibits both magnetic and semi-conductive properties, making it a suitable candidate for applications involving both memory and photovoltaic technology. Furthermore, by examining various configurations, we found that both N and C can form a bond with a titanium atom in a octahedral configuration if there is an absence or reduction of oxygen, resulting in a semi-conductive arrangement, and when situated in a site where it can form a bond with a titanium atom in a tetrahedral configuration, it results in a magnetic and semi-conductive arrangement. This indicates that both N and C can be utilized as p-elements to dope TiO2, making it a suitable material for applications involving memory and photovoltaic technology. This research was conducted using the Fleur package with the full-polarized method within the 10^-8 Ry accuracy range. In collisions of high-energy protons, identifying the creation of top-quark pairs can be challenging due to being overwhelmed by abundant background noise.  A promising approach for extracting these events involves analyzing specific patterns of particle scattering, particularly elastic proton-proton collisions, where the collision products are confined to one side of the detector.  By utilizing data from the Large Hadron Collider, researchers propose a method that combines data from both sides of the detector to search for signs of elastic top-quark pair production, potentially shedding light on the exact size of the top-quark's cross-sectional area.  This study utilizes comprehensive software simulations incorporating real LHC data and sheds new light on the properties of the large hadron collider's elastic process, specifically the behavior of forward-scattered particles.  Further studies on elastic processes at the Large Hadron Collider may also provide valuable insights into the characteristics of forward-scattered particles, facilitating a deeper understanding of the collider itself.

A novel employment for simulating massless Dirac fermions in (1+1)D space is proposed, leveraging quantum circuits with excess ancilla qubits. Originally, quantum circuit simulations are limited by the inevitability of decoherence from interactions with their environment. By employing qutrits instead of qubits, the rate of this decoherence is significantly reduced, although it inevitably leads to circuit complexity and a resulting time-dependent effect on the simulation results. A strategy is presented to mitigate this impact by adopting a suitable initial state for the ancilla qutrits, one that minimizes the effect of decoherence on key spectral properties of the simulated model. As a specific application, this method is shown to efficiently simulate the dimerized su(2) chain, a well-studied model with both semi-Dirac and gapped phases, by analyzing spectral gaps, spectral widths, and energy spectra obtained from time-evolved simulations. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of small-scale, noise-sensitive quantum devices in accurately simulating complex systems and provides a framework for effectively utilizing qutrits as ancillas in quantum simulations. The research is further expanded to explore the integration of discrete time-modulated driving protocols that accurately simulate the interaction of fermionic systems with external influences, offering a more realistic and precise simulation of real-world systems. The findings are relevant to a broader context, extending far beyond qutrit-based simulations to covering general principles applicable to noise-induced errors in quantum simulations, including those employing qubits. The research is accompanied by publicly accessible code, available at https://github.com/Quantum-Group/sQED-simulation. The code utilizes the QuTip++ library, a Python framework for solving the time-evolved open quantum systems. The research was conducted without the aid of a supercomputer, demonstrating the feasibility of simulations on mid-range hardware. The results of the simulations are presented in the accompanying figures, which include the calculated spectra obtained from time-evolved simulations, as well as energy spectra obtained via numerical analysis, and are also summarized in the tables provided. The flow of liquids through porous media is influenced by surface roughness, especially at high velocities where friction becomes a significant issue. In this study, we examine the surface roughness of dish soap films divided into symmetric and asymmetric categories. By manipulating the geometry of these films, we can determine the resistance they encounter. Our findings show that the films' resistance is 20 times greater than frictionless expectations, with the surface roughness accounting for most of this extra resistance. Additionally, our research indicates that the films' resistance can be the same regardless of whether they have channels that cross or not, demonstrating a topological immunity to change. Furthermore, our data reveal that the films' resistance is 5 times greater than expected when there are sharp corners present, with the reduction of extra resistance occurring when the velocity is increased. Our study also compares its results with other models and finds that the films' resistance is similar to that of rough pipes but unlike them does not become negligible at high velocities. Our research spans a wide range of velocities, surface tensions, and soap concentrations, all while accounting for the roughness's effect on the flow and the resulting geometry. Our data show that the flow in these films is viscous rather than laminar, which is supported by both visual observations and measurements of channel widths. Our findings can be used to create an accurate model of the films' resistance that takes into account their geometric characteristics, the flow's velocity, the surface tension, and the viscosity of the liquid. Our model's validation occurs through the comparison of our calculated measurements against our actual measurements of the films' resistance. In neural machine translation, a common issue arises when the source sentence contains references to objects that have not been introduced in previous sentences. Research has explored methods to extend neural machine translation to handle such cases, but successful applications are limited to simple situations like describing iconic scenes. In contrast, our focus expansion model targets more challenging creation tasks, including generating fictional characters, crafting poems, and designing artificial objects. Unlike existing approaches that directly map input elements to output words, our model employs a target word as a guide to determine a focused element, which is then used to generate the desired output. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that our focus expansion model effectively produces coherent and meaningful creations by interacting with neural machine translation, yet it struggles to achieve high fidelity with regard to input specifications. To overcome this limitation, we integrate our model with neural machine translation, resulting in the focused generation neural machine interpretation framework. In this framework, the model first produces a partial representation of the desired object before generating the corresponding text, which allows us to create more complex scenes with higher fidelity. The evaluation shows that our approach outperforms existing methods in various creation tasks. The model code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/focused-generation. The data used during this study are available due to the dedicated nature of the work, which includes generating fictional characters, crafting poems, and designing artificial objects, and are therefore not publicly uploadable, but similar datasets can be created according to the guidelines provided. The evaluation was conducted on three creation datasets: the fictional character dataset, the poem dataset, and the object generation dataset. Our study focused on three areas of investigation: the relationship between the J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio and other processes such as form factors, hadron decay widths, and dark matter annihilation; the impact of assumptions about hadron decay widths, especially for the decay of the charmed meson D0, which is subject to limited experimental data; and the effect of using different effective field theories, such as the standard model and the two-Higgs-doublet model, in calculating the J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio. We found that in the standard model and the two-Histogram-doublet model, the J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio is significantly certain, while in the other two scenarios, which include the vector neutrino model, uncertainty prevails. On the other hand, we investigated the consequences of assuming a large J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio, which is beyond the current experimental limit, and found that it would result in a complete inefficiency in using J/ψ data to search for light neutrinos and dark energy. We also analyzed the relationship between the J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio and other processes such as form factors, hadron decay widths, and dark matter annihilation, which are crucial for understanding hadron decay widths, especially for the decay of the charmed meson D0, which is subject to limited experimental data. We concluded that in the standard model and the two-Histogram-doublet model, the J/ψ to invisible matter branching ratio is significantly certain, while in the other two scenarios, which include the vector neutrino model, uncertainty prevails. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a random walk in one dimension, focusing on the time it takes for the walk to leave a confined space and the characteristics of its path during this period. Unlike previous studies that examined the walk's asymptotic behavior beyond a given boundary, we consider the walk's dynamics when it is first confined to a specific space and explore the time it takes to escape that space and the features of its path during this escape period. Our primary finding is that there is a critical threshold, dependent on the walk's initial conditions, beyond which the walk's duration within the restricted space follows a power law with a specific exponent, and we provide a clear expression for this exponent. Furthermore, we show that the walk's path during the escape period can be characterized by a specific probability distribution that is independent of the walk's initial conditions, and we identify this distribution as the geometric distribution's second moment, which has a distinct parameter that is dependent on the walk's initial conditions. Notably, our results build on previous findings by the authors in "Random Walk's Last Exit" and "First Passage Time's Probability Density". The key approach used in this research involves applying a transformation that converts the walk's space-time trajectory into a new trajectory that allows for the application of the stochastic integral transformation, which in turn enables the derivation of the walk's duration's probability density from its trajectory. The research also includes an analytical solution for the walk's duration's density, which is validated by the results obtained from numerical simulations. The model under investigation has been compared to a related model called the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process, which is a second-order Markov chain, and the differences between these two models have been highlighted. The research further explores the walk's duration's distribution's properties, which include its moment-generating function, its cumulant-generating function, and its central moment, as well as the application of the Feller's test to the walk's duration's density. The results obtained in this research are applicable to a broader class of models called the subdiffusive processes, which include the walk under investigation. The IShTAR plasma generator at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany is a key component for testing and validating materials for fusion reactors. A study was conducted to understand the plasma produced by the generator's helicon source, with particular focus on verifying its operation in the helicon regime. To achieve this, a multi-method approach was employed, utilizing spectroscopic analysis, interposed neutral filters, and a camera to capture visible light. Plasma parameters were determined through modeling and matching of experimental data, with results indicating the generator produces plasma in the helicon regime with plasma densities ranging from 10^11 to 10^12 particles per cubic centimeter. Furthermore, a comparison was drawn with operating characteristics of commercial helicon sources, demonstrating that the IShTAR generator's anatomy facilitates efficient plasma production even in a large chamber. Overall, this study has enhanced the understanding of the IShTAR generator and provides a reliable framework for validating materials for fusion reactors.

In recent years, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant traction in processing complex graph data, with applications in vital areas such as social network analysis and molecular chemistry study. To advance our understanding of these networks, our research delves into the theoretical aspects of basic GCNN models by directly linking their convolution operations to classic signal processing techniques. Concretely, we demonstrate that graph convolution operations are equivalent to applying a specific signal processing method called'matched filtering' followed by a linear transformation. Through this analysis, we gain a deeper insight into how GCNNs process data, which can be utilized to address pressing issues such as verifying the validity of GCNNs for handling noisy data and evaluating their performance when input is corrupted. To address these challenges, we develop a new detection mechanism called the 'Validability Detector' which can be an valuable tool for identifying the conditions under which GCNNs remain effective in real-world scenarios. We also conduct an exhaustive set of experiments to prove the practical utility of our analysis. To summarize, our research provides a novel perspective on the fundamental workings of basic GCNNs, presents a new validation criterion for GCNNs, and presents a precise methodology for analyzing GCNNs. We believe that our approach can be an valuable foundation for developing more robust and accurate GCNN models. In the context of online learning, the $k$-means clustering algorithm groups $k$ objects into clusters based on their feature vectors, with the aim of minimizing the within-cluster variance. However, implementing this algorithm is challenging due to the need for frequent recalculation of cluster centers and identification of significant changes in data. To address this issue, we developed a revised algorithm called Dynamic $k$-means Grouping, which detects and adapts to changes in data by employing a thresholded system similar to ExpGrowth, while guaranteeing nearly optimal performance in terms of variance and cluster centers' distance from their optimal counterparts. Specifically, our results show that the algorithm can maintain clusters that are within a factor of $O(\sqrt{k}\cdot \sigma \cdot t^{1/4})$ from the optimal variance and cluster centers' distance, where $\sigma$ represents the dimension of the feature space and $t$ denotes time. Moreover, cluster centers can be updated in $O(k^{3/2} \cdot \sigma^{3/2} \cdot \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)} \cdot \sqrt{t})$ time, with probabilities of failure less than $\delta$. We have also introduced a variance-clustering tree data structure, which is more efficient in terms of memory usage and allows for faster query processing. Finally, our algorithm's performance has been compared with existing dynamic $k$-means algorithms, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of variance and cluster centers' distance from their optimal counterparts. This has been substantiated through extensive simulations conducted using both synthetic and real-world data. Lastly, we have outlined possible modifications to the algorithm, as well as its potential applications in various contexts. In a wide-ranging class of multi-agent games, known as pursuit-withdrawal games, certain agents, called pursuers, aim to reach all nodes within a given stochastic network, while others, called hideaways, avoid being discovered at specific nodes. Research on these games typically focuses on a simple structure, where agents can choose between one of two nodes. By extending this framework to more complex networks with hierarchical divisions, our current study explores strategies for optimizing the deployment of pursuers to reach all nodes, while accounting for the hiding behavior of withdrawaways. Our proposed approach utilizes a new version of the algebraic approach to solve complex stochastic hierarchical problems, showcasing its capabilities on a variety of test cases. Our research also provides a clear pathway for investigating larger-scale hierarchical problems. Our findings are further validated through simulations, which demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in scaling to larger networks. Our research on the algebraic method highlights the potential for its application in solving a broad range of complex stochastic hierarchical problems across various fields. Our work on the hierarchical network is also presented as a specialized case of a more general network, which can be represented as a set of hierarchical sub-networks, offering a new hierarchical perspective that may be useful for various real-world applications, such as transportation, supply chain management, and telecommunications. Our current research can be used to address a range of issues in these fields, including but not limited to finding the most efficient paths in hierarchical networks, optimizing resource allocation across different layers of a hierarchical network, and identifying areas of interest within complex spatial networks. Our approach provides a versatile framework for solving these problems, as demonstrated on a variety of test cases. Our research on the algebraic method and hierarchical networks has also been presented at the International Conference on Decision and Game Theory for Logic and Psychology. In our research, we delved into complex multi-task reinforcement learning, focusing on scenarios where tasks are highly interdependent and require integration through shared components. To simulate this process, we created a training environment consisting of multiple modular systems that interact with each on the basis of their individual component structures. Our primary discovery took place within a specially designed grid world, comprising both agent modules and environment modules that followed a deterministic pattern. Interestingly, when the environment modules changed unexpectedly, we found that the agent modules that formed a closed system were remarkably resilient and adapted quickly, even exhibiting improved performance. Our analysis revealed that this adaptation was directly linked to the internal consistency of their own sub-systems and the way they interact with the environment modules. To validate our findings, we tested this resilience in various other setups, including non-deterministic scenarios, and found that the agents' ability to adapt was unique to the most complex scenario. Our research contributes a rich set of data to the field of multi-task reinforcement learning, particularly in relation to the resistance of complex systems to disruption. Our associated code is available online.

We introduce a novel algorithm for an unbounded number of agents to gather at a specific point (0,0) in a weighted graph, and we prove this algorithm is optimal in terms of speed for agents on a one-dimensional line. We then demonstrate how this gathering algorithm can be applied to various network configurations, and we show it satisfies certain safety and liveness properties. Additionally, we provide a statistical analysis of a random search strategy. Lastly, we explore the implications of our results for the fundamental question of whether it is possible to create a reliable navigation system based solely on partial map information. In solving inverse problems, the goal is to restore a clean and clear image given a noisy and distorted input. This research focuses on an essential yet under-explored area of inverse problems - those where the level of distortion is significant, as seen in image forgery detection, compressive sensing-based image reconstruction from heavily degraded data, and restoring heavily manipulated or doctored images. A major limitation in conventional GAN-based inverse problems is the lack of controllable noise, which hinders efficient training and makes it difficult to generate high-quality inverses. To overcome this challenge, we introduce an innovative regularized conditional GAN framework that produces a clean and accurate inverse by controlling the noise in the input. The proposed network consists of a standard conditional GAN, a noise-aware encoder, and a noise controller. This paper presents a generative text-to-speech model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to address limitations in current neural network-based waveform generative models. By integrating a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network as the feature extractor, QPNet successfully captures the pitch or periodic information from raw waveform inputs. Unlike previous models, it does not rely on external pitch estimates, allowing non-autoregressive and efficient training. Furthermore, a thresholded dilated convolution approach is proposed to incorporate external pitch information while preserving the spatial learning ability. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of QPNet in generating high-fidelity speech, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in various evaluation metrics. Code is available at: https://github.com/EchoSeh/QPNet.

The bicategorical invariants previously developed by the first author, notably the Bock-Tannaka formalism and the theory of shadows, are reviewed. A key aspect of these tools is their capacity to distinguish between bicategorical representations. A crucial discovery is then presented, demonstrating that the presence of certain specific marks on a bicategorical functor is equivalent to it being indistinguishable from another functor, one that lacks those marks. In essence, such marks have no substantive impact and can be considered cosmetic. A straightforward, albeit somewhat abstract, example of this concept is provided. Furthermore, more complex instances involving symmetric bicategorical representations are discussed, including a notable case involving the ADE series. A connection to the theory of symmetries of Dynkin diagrams is established. A related result, obtained by modifying the Bock-Tannaka approach, is also presented. This modification enables the development of certain specific marks that possess actual and distinguishing consequences. This leads to the discovery of marks that have a physically interpretable effect, Demazure operators, which Demazure initially proposed in the context of Lie algebras. These operator marks exhibit a combinatorial impact that can be determined through the examination of Hasse diagrams. They also demonstrate a capacity for categorizing the finite subalgebras of Yangian algebras, which Yang and Bazhan introduced. This leads to the discovery of previously unrecognized structures on the set of these subalgebras, namely the relation of lower cover and Demazure operators. This relationship can be visually represented as a diagram. This finding also leads to the interpretation of Coxeter groups as groups of operator marks. This includes the finite Coxeter groups, which were previously defined by Bourbaki. This research was conducted as part of the project ``From Marks to Algebras'', which aims to explore the relationship between bicategorical invariants and the underlying geometric properties of the spaces they act upon. This relationship is conceptual in nature and involves the conversion of topological spaces into algebras through the use of combinatorial marks. In response to this trend, this study introduces a novel concept, Lorentzian graph neural networks, which incorporates Lorentzian transformation, a lesser-known non-linear transformation, that can be effectively employed for optimizing deep learning models. Specifically, we demonstrate how embedding Lorentzian transformation within GNN architectures leads to better performance in comparison to conventional real-valued and complex-valued networks, as evidenced by our experimental findings across six well-known datasets. Moreover, the analysis of our study provides a potential non-linear substitute for the widely-used complex-valued network, which can be utilized in various neural network applications.
